## 1. Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Climate finance, that is North-South financial flows directed at mitigating and adapting to climate change, has become a centerpiece of climate change conferences. Yet the scholarship discussing it remains bibliographically fragmented. It includes both academic publications, dispersed across databases with different coverage profiles, and institutional publications from the likes of the UNFCCC (diplomatic negotiation records), the OECD (bilateral and multilateral finance guidelines and statistics), or the Climate Policy Initiative (think tanks reports) sitting out of standard academic databases. The literature is also multilingual: while English dominates, a monolingual approach risks missing entirely the multicultural and Southern perspectives.

Pioneering bibliometric work has begun to map this terrain. @care_weber2023 survey climate finance using Scopus; @shang_jin2023 analyse climate finance from Web of Science; @maria_etal2023 map green finance with network analysis. These studies rely on a single database each, search in English only, and they publish only the OpenAlex query, not the reusable dataset. The present work addresses these limitations: a climate finance corpus built from {{< meta corpus_sources >}} complementary sources, with a documented quality-filtering pipeline, and multilingual with sentence-transformer embeddings that place all works in a shared semantic space regardless of language. Because "climate finance" is a contested category whose boundaries are themselves an object of study, we err on the side of inclusion and publish a much larger corpus than the three references above. As we filter out pure green finance to retain only works related to international climate finance, the present corpus subsumes 89.3% of the works retrieved for @care_weber2023's published query and 91.0% for @shang_jin2023's (queries replicated against OpenAlex, matched by DOI and year-constrained title; probe of 2026-07-22), and 40.1% of @maria_etal2023's, which spans green finance at large --- a broader field than this dataset covers by design.

The dataset was constructed for a history-of-economic-thought study of how climate finance was born as an economic aggregate [Ha-Duong, under review], but its scope makes it reusable for topic modelling, citation network analysis, bibliometric mapping, and cross-lingual studies. For example, it can replicate several previous findings:

- @kouwenberg_zheng2023 report exponential growth in climate finance publications, especially from 2015 onwards; we confirm the take-off, with a structural break in the trend of log annual corpus counts at 2015 (Chow F = {{< meta lit_growth_f >}}, p {{< meta lit_growth_p >}}) and output growing {{< meta lit_growth_post_pct >}}% a year since.
- @kouwenberg_zheng2023 also find the financial--economic author cluster "quite disconnected" from the rest of the field; we confirm on citation links. After clustering on cocitations, edges between the public-finance pole (allocation, governance, loss-and-damage) and the market-finance pole (climate risk, green bonds, innovation finance) make up {{< meta lit_poles_cross_pct >}}% of edges against {{< meta lit_poles_cross_null_pct >}}% expected under degree-preserving rewiring (z = {{< meta lit_poles_z >}}, p {{< meta lit_poles_p >}}).
- @diazrainey_etal2017 found that very few climate finance articles appeared in top finance journals between 1998 and mid-2015. Our corpus confirms the near-absence and dates the turn, with the finance-journal share of corpus works rising from {{< meta lit_finshare_pre_pct >}}% before 2015 to {{< meta lit_finshare_post_pct >}}% after.

## 2. Method {#sec-method}

### 2.1 Sources {#sec-sources}

The corpus assembles academic and grey literature from {{< meta corpus_sources >}} sources with complementary coverage profiles (@tbl-sources). Five are automated or semi-automated (reproducible from the scripts and an internet connection); three require manual export from restricted platforms.

| Source | Automation | Coverage |
|--------|------------|----------|
| OpenAlex [@priem_etal2022] | Automated (free API) | Primary academic source (indexes Crossref, DOAJ, PubMed, and more): tiered keyword search |
| ISTEX | Automated (public API) | CNRS national text-mining platform (multi-publisher) |
| Grey literature | Hybrid (curated seed + World Bank API) | 17 curated reports [e.g., @buchner2013] + World Bank repository |
| Teaching canon | AI-assisted (scraping + LLM extraction) | Syllabus readings from university courses worldwide |
| bibCNRS | Hand-harvested (CNRS credentials) | CNRS portal aggregating non-English news & discourse (Gale, Wanfang, NewsBank) in FR, ZH, JA, DE |
| SciSpace | AI-collected, hand-exported | SciSpace systematic review tool exports |
| UNFCCC | AI-collected | Negotiation documents  |
| OECD | Hand-harvested | Statistical guidelines |

: Sources, automation level, and coverage scope. {#tbl-sources}

The search strategy uses a four-tier keyword taxonomy reflecting the evolving vocabulary of climate finance: core terms in eight languages (Tier 1), English institutional and diplomatic vocabulary (Tier 2), and climate-adjacent terms with co-occurrence filters to maintain precision (Tiers 3--4). The taxonomy was informed by keyword mining of {{< meta corpus_core >}} core papers (cited $\geq$ {{< meta corpus_core_threshold >}} times). It is retrospective by construction: mined from the vocabulary the field settled on, it embeds the negotiation calendar in the harvest itself --- a circularity to keep in mind when dating the field's turns from this corpus alone.

All API queries are bounded to publication years 1990--2024; the lower bound reflects the start of UNFCCC negotiations, before which "climate finance" had no institutional referent. OpenAlex indexes economics working papers from RePEc, NBER, MPRA, and other repositories, so no separate harvest is needed. Sources bibCNRS and SciSpace together contribute 896 records to the raw pool before quality filtering (@tbl-quality); the bibCNRS aggregates capture non-English public discourse absent from academic databases. For UNFCCC (225 records) and OECD (33 records) documents available in multiple languages, we index only the English version.

### 2.2 Data Structure {#sec-data-structure}

The merge pipeline combines records from all sources through two deduplication passes: DOI-based (normalised, lowercased), which removes {{< meta dedup_doi_removed >}} records, and title+year matching for records lacking DOIs, which removes a further {{< meta dedup_titleyear_removed >}}. When duplicates are found, the maximum citation count is retained and metadata follows a source-priority order. Boolean `from_*` columns (one per source) track which databases contributed each record, enabling provenance analysis. The `source_count` field records multi-source agreement: of the {{< meta corpus_total >}} refined works, {{< meta corpus_multi_source >}} ({{< meta corpus_multi_source_pct >}}%) appear in multiple sources.

A six-flag filtering pipeline then evaluates every work. Three flags require no external data: (1) missing metadata (no title), (2) absent abstract combined with an irrelevant title (lacking domain-specific terms in any of the target languages), and (3) title blacklist matches (noise terms such as "blockchain" or "deep learning" without climate-finance context). Three flags depend on enrichment outputs: (4) citation isolation (pre-2020 works neither cited by nor citing any other corpus work), (5) semantic outlier detection (embedding distance from corpus centroid exceeding mean + 2 standard deviations), and (6) cross-encoder relevance scoring against the query "climate policy and financial mechanisms."

A separate annotation step detects near-duplicate content: coordinated multi-journal publications where the same text appears under different DOIs. Detection uses a two-pass approach (abstract prefix clustering followed by title clustering with abstract-similarity validation) and assigns a shared `near_duplicate_group` identifier. These records are kept, not removed: they are real publications.

The pipeline removes flagged works unless they meet one of four protection criteria: citation count $\geq$ 50, presence in 2+ sources, within-corpus citations, or appearance in teaching syllabi. The teaching canon was built by scraping university course syllabi worldwide and extracting bibliographic references through a combination of DOI regex matching and LLM-assisted extraction, followed by fuzzy deduplication and Crossref enrichment (details in the companion technical report). Every inclusion/exclusion decision is recorded in the audit trail.

### 2.3 Quality, Completeness, and Potential Biases {#sec-quality}

@tbl-quality summarises corpus composition and metadata completeness per source. The "Refined" column counts works with a `from_*` provenance flag after deduplication and quality filtering; a single work may appear in multiple rows if discovered by several sources. %non-EN is the share of non-English works, %DOI the share with a valid DOI, %Abstract the share with an abstract longer than 50 characters, and %Refs the share with at least one reference in the citation graph.

{{< include ../_shared/tables/tab_corpus_sources.md >}}

The merge pipeline reduces {{< meta corpus_raw >}} raw records to {{< meta corpus_total >}} refined works ({{< meta corpus_removal_pct >}}% removal rate). Of the {{< meta filter_flagged >}} works flagged (counts are non-exclusive: a single work may trigger multiple flags), citation isolation ({{< meta filter_citation_isolated >}}) and cross-encoder relevance scoring ({{< meta filter_llm_irrelevant >}}) are the most common, followed by absent abstracts with irrelevant titles ({{< meta filter_no_abstract >}}), missing metadata ({{< meta filter_missing_metadata >}}), and title blacklist matches ({{< meta filter_title_blacklist >}}). Of these, {{< meta filter_protected >}} are retained by protection criteria, yielding {{< meta filter_net_removals >}} net removals; an additional 21 content-duplicates discovered during enrichment are also removed.

As @tbl-quality shows, OpenAlex contributes {{< meta openalex_pct >}}% of refined works; the seven smaller sources increase the corpus's non-English, institutional, and pedagogical coverage. Citation graph verification on a sample of 300 links confirmed 99.0% against Crossref metadata (95% CI [97.1%, 99.7%]); the 1% unconfirmed are OpenAlex-sourced references absent from Crossref, not errors. Restricting to links where both works belong to the refined corpus yields {{< meta cite_refined_rows >}} corpus-internal citation pairs, covering {{< meta cite_refined_coverage_pct >}}% of corpus DOIs ({{< meta cite_coverage_core_pct >}}% for core papers).

Complete reference lists are another matter. Among the {{< meta refs_doi_docs >}} DOI-bearing works, the median number of references contributed to the citation graph is {{< meta refs_median >}} (mean {{< meta refs_mean >}}, 95th percentile {{< meta refs_p95 >}}, maximum {{< meta refs_max >}}); {{< meta refs_zero_n >}} works ({{< meta refs_zero_share_pct >}}%) contribute none, a gap concentrated in books, reviews, editorials, and grey literature, while counts in the hundreds mark review articles. Absence of outgoing links measures indexing, not scholarly isolation; per-document reference counts are the screening variable to check before any citation-based analysis.

Relevance filtering (flag 6) uses a cross-encoder reranker (BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3) with the query "climate policy and financial mechanisms"; human validation on a blinded sample of 100 works yielded AUC = 0.818 and 81% accuracy. The boundary is threshold-sensitive: halving or doubling the score threshold reclassifies roughly 10% of the calibration sample either way, so counts of "climate finance" works inherit the threshold choice; the deposited calibration table lets users move it. The chosen query privileges instrumental framing, and the scores are not ground truth, since what counts as "climate finance" is itself contested. The Zenodo deposit includes all calibration and validation tables.

{{< include ../_shared/tables/tab_languages.md >}}

Users should be aware of several potential biases. The corpus is strongest on the academic pool and weakest on policy discourse and media, partially captured through the grey-literature and bibCNRS sources. Non-English coverage remains limited (@tbl-languages): English accounts for {{< meta lang_english_pct >}}% of refined works despite targeting eight languages, reflecting structural biases in indexing systems; the non-English layer counts 3,381 works, led by Portuguese, Spanish, German, and French --- enough for case studies rather than balanced cross-language comparisons. Citation counts reflect OpenAlex data as of 2026-07-24 and favour older, English-language works; the teaching canon is biased toward institutions with publicly accessible syllabi, and its LLM extraction step has not been independently audited.

The grey-literature source is scoped to international institutions (the UNFCCC system, the OECD, the World Bank, transnational think tanks) and deliberately excludes documents from national institutions: government reports, economic analysis councils, central bank communications. The boundary follows the research object --- climate finance as an economic aggregate for international economic governance, constituted in the UNFCCC and OECD arenas --- and tractability. We acknowledge that the exclusion costs multi-cultural coverage, since these institutions are dominated by OECD countries. The corpus could be complemented with regional databases such as CNKI for Chinese journals, where domestic scholarship on green finance is extensive, SciELO for Latin American journals, where Brazilian scholarship on green and climate finance is active, or Garuda for Indonesian journals, for example. The data harvesting pipeline is also available, and can accept additional sources to extend the corpus without reprocessing existing ones.

### 2.4 OpenAlex limitations and pipeline responses {#sec-openalex-limits}

OpenAlex offers the widest coverage of any open scholarly database and indexes working papers, but its metadata quality is uneven [@priem_etal2022]. It supplies {{< meta openalex_pct >}}% of refined works, so each documented flaw deserves its response — the pipeline step that addresses it, or the statement that none does.

Keyword queries return false positives. The six-flag filter (@sec-data-structure) is the response; its cross-encoder relevance scoring was human-validated at AUC = 0.818 (@sec-quality).

Duplicate records are the residual weak point. Two passes deduplicate at merge (DOI-based, then title+year), and `near_duplicate_group` annotates same-content works published under distinct DOIs. Some working paper / published version pairs still slip through: works sharing an exact normalised title and first-author surname but published up to five years apart form {{< meta dedup_fn_pairs >}} candidate pairs ({{< meta dedup_fn_pairs_pct >}}% of works), about half of them genuine version pairs; fuzzy title matching raises the upper bound to {{< meta dedup_fn_upper_docs >}} works ({{< meta dedup_fn_upper_pct >}}%), a tier dominated by distinct report editions. The passes also over-merge occasionally: {{< meta dedup_fp_doi_collision_groups >}} DOI groups join records with unrelated titles, and the title+year key merges {{< meta dedup_fp_empty_year_docs >}} generically titled empty-year works into {{< meta dedup_fp_empty_year_groups >}} groups. The direction of the residual bias is known: surviving version pairs double-count citations, inflating co-citation and community-size statistics. Author metadata is itself noisy across sources, so author-normalised deduplication is left to a future release. The audit script and its output table (`tab_dedup_error_estimates.csv`) ship with the pipeline code.

The abstract field concentrates two flaws. Abstracts are often missing: enrichment reconstructs them from OpenAlex inverted indices and ISTEX fulltext, and residual absences trigger flag 2. Stored abstracts are sometimes contaminated, holding boilerplate (paywall notices, repository metadata) or the article's own text: boilerplate detection excludes stub abstracts from the embeddings, and oversize detection excludes full-text fields.

Citation assignments can be incorrect; the audit reported in @sec-quality confirmed 99.0% of sampled links, the rest being OpenAlex-sourced references absent from Crossref rather than errors.

Reference lists arrive empty or aberrant; per-document reference counts (@sec-quality) are the screening variable, and GROBID parses the unstructured reference strings Crossref and OpenAlex leave unresolved (@sec-data). The audit above verifies the links we have, not the links we miss: with a fifth of DOI-bearing works contributing no outgoing edge, network statistics should be checked for sensitivity to their exclusion.

Missing full-text is not mitigated: we do not hold the full texts of the corpus's academic works, so the citation graph relies on indexed metadata and deposited reference strings, and no-DOI works (24%) are undercounted.

## 3. Data description {#sec-data}

The Zenodo deposit (DOI: [10.5281/zenodo.19236130](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19236130), temporal coverage 1990--2024) is a reproducibility archive in three parts: the pipeline source code (`code/`: scripts, configuration, and DVC definitions), the raw data inputs (`data/inputs/`: the six per-source catalogs as harvested, before merge and deduplication), and the final data products of this paper (`data/products/`: the v1.1 corpus files described below). All CSV files use UTF-8 encoding with standard comma-separated format; identifiers are opaque string keys.

**climate_finance_corpus.csv** ({{< meta corpus_raw >}} rows). The complete, unfiltered corpus: one deduplicated work per row, every column described in @tbl-variables and in the deposited codebook (`codebook.md`), which adds per-column allowed values and measured missingness. The quality flags are the audit trail: users reproduce our refined subset ({{< meta corpus_total >}} works) with `df[~df['is_flagged'] | df['is_protected']]`. The `near_duplicate_group` column identifies coordinated multi-journal publications sharing near-identical content; `in_v1` marks works present in the v1.0 submission corpus. Abstracts are not included in the deposited file due to publisher redistribution restrictions; they can be retrieved programmatically via the DOI or OpenAlex identifier --- which means reuse re-fetches them from a live index that drifts, unlike the frozen fields deposited here. @fig-bars shows the temporal distribution.

{{< include ../_shared/tables/tab_variables.md >}}

**embeddings.npz.** Compressed NumPy archive (keys: `vectors` as float32 array, `keys` as string array of identifiers) containing L2-normalised (unit-length) {{< meta emb_dimensions >}}-dimensional vectors for {{< meta corpus_with_embeddings >}} of the {{< meta corpus_raw >}} works, computed by the multilingual sentence-transformer *BAAI/bge-m3*. Works without a title are excluded; works with missing or boilerplate abstracts (paywall stubs, repository metadata) are embedded from title and keywords only. Row *i* of `vectors` corresponds to `keys[i]`. Flagged works are included to support alternative filtering strategies. Each vector encodes the concatenation of title, abstract (when available and non-boilerplate), and keywords within the model's 8192-token context window (no truncation for typical abstracts). The model maps texts in English, French, Chinese, Japanese, and German into a shared semantic space, which is designed to group works by topic rather than by language. These vectors serve as direct input for BERTopic, top2vec, or other embedding-based topic models, and support cosine-similarity search.

**citations.csv.** Citation network ({{< meta cite_total_rows >}} rows). Columns: `source_doi`, `ref_doi` (both normalised, lowercased DOIs). Each row records a (citing, cited) pair where the citing work belongs to the corpus; the cited work may or may not. For corpus-internal citations only, join on the corpus identifiers. The citation network operates on DOI pairs: works without DOIs cannot be matched as citing sources, and references without DOIs are retained but cannot be deduplicated. Since 24% of records lack DOIs, citation coverage is incomplete for early and grey-literature works. The pipeline applies GROBID at the reference-string level: `corpus_parse_citations_grobid.py` (in the deposited code) parses the free-text citation strings that Crossref and OpenAlex return unresolved, recovering title, first author, and year, which a fuzzy-matching step then resolves against corpus works. Full-text reference extraction — parsing the PDF of every corpus document — is not performed, because we do not hold the full texts of the academic works; GROBID therefore operates on deposited reference strings across the whole corpus, not on PDFs.

**Source catalogs.** Per-source catalogs (`openalex_works.csv`, `istex_works.csv`, etc.), shipped under `data/inputs/`, enable provenance tracking back to individual databases before merge and deduplication. The corpus does not include a dedicated Open Access or fulltext URL column; users can recover OA links via the OpenAlex API using the `source_id` field, or construct ISTEX fulltext URLs from ISTEX identifiers in the source catalogs.

The dataset is released under CC BY 4.0. The five automated or semi-automated sources can be re-harvested with an internet connection; the three restricted sources (bibCNRS, SciSpace, OECD) have their raw exports included in the Zenodo deposit.

## 4. Descriptive statistics {#sec-descriptive}

![Annual publication volume in the corpus (light bars) and the subset with the phrase "climate finance" in title or abstract (dark segments). The phrase is nearly absent before 2009, then spreads through the literature. Background bands mark the three periods (before 2007, crystallisation, established field); labels flag the Rio Convention (1992), the Bali Action Plan (2007), and the Paris Agreement (2015). The search window is 1990--2024; the earliest works date from 1992.](../_shared/figures/fig_bars.png){#fig-bars width=100%}

Citation coverage --- the share of corpus works that appear as a citing source in the citation network --- is unevenly distributed over time: approximately 27% for works published before 2007 versus 47% for post-2015 works. <!-- TODO(v2 numbers): 27%/47% are v1.0 figures; on the v2 corpus a quick recomputation gives ~86%/77% (GROBID + catalog-stage reference layers lifted early-period coverage). Regenerate from the canonical artifact and rewrite this paragraph, including the direction of the gradient. --> This gap reflects two compounding factors: early and grey-literature works are less likely to carry DOIs or to have their reference lists indexed by Crossref and OpenAlex, and the field itself was smaller before 2007. Users conducting temporal citation-network analyses should account for this systematic undercount of early-period connectivity.

The companion study [Ha-Duong, under review] partitions the field into six semantic clusters. k-means with k = 6 on the present corpus and its 1024-dimensional embeddings (against 384 dimensions in v1.0) recovers five of the six themes, with a land-use cluster emerging in place of the \$100bn/fund-flows theme, and the partition is stable across estimation variants (adjusted Rand index (ARI) $\geq$ {{< meta lit_sem6_ari >}} between raw, normalised, and restart variants over {{< meta lit_sem6_n >}} works).
The two structurations of the corpus --- citation communities (@fig-global-map) and semantic clusters (@fig-sem-composition) --- do not correspond one for one: communities that share a vocabulary do not necessarily cite each other.

@fig-global-map shows what the citation network resolves at full-corpus scale: Louvain community detection on the intra-corpus citation graph yields {{< meta gm_communities >}} major communities covering {{< meta gm_coverage_pct >}}% of the {{< meta gm_n_connected >}} connected works. The communities correspond to recognisable research programmes, from carbon markets to green bonds; the companion paper [Ha-Duong, under review] develops this community-level analysis.

## 5. Concluding Remarks {#sec-concluding}

This corpus assembles climate finance scholarship into a single, cross-lingual bibliographic object. Its {{< meta corpus_sources >}}-source design pairs the breadth of OpenAlex with coverage from French archives (ISTEX), non-English discourse (bibCNRS), institutional reports (grey literature), pedagogical use (teaching canon), and AI-assisted discovery (SciSpace).

Can such a corpus serve the history of economic thought? The companion paper [Ha-Duong, under review] is the proof of use. It argues that climate finance crystallised as a category of economic governance around 2009, and assigns the corpus a deliberately modest epistemic role: the quantitative evidence corroborates a history built from documents, actors, and dates. Structural-break detection on the yearly embedding distributions, blind to the negotiation calendar, finds its main rupture at 2007; lexical methods date when the field's terms entered and left use; plain descriptive statistics do honest work.

The referee's caution deserves a candid reply: any focused research question will demand task-specific cleaning beyond the generic filtering documented here. The corpus is reusable infrastructure, not a finished analysis, and our own use shows both the limit and what survives it. Community-separation tests fail on the pre-2007 window --- fewer than 50 works per year is too thin a base for any statistic to escape its null. Yet qualitative results stand on simple counts: @negishi1960, the welfare-weights framework one would expect to anchor burden-sharing debates, is absent from the corpus's pre-2007 canon, while Scott Barrett's treaty-participation economics [@barrett2003participation] is co-cited with the carbon-pricing literature rather than with institutionalist scholarship. Where inference runs out, description still speaks.

Beyond this programme, the provenance and author metadata support networks of institutions and co-authors, the embeddings feed topic models and content classification, and the multilingual design permits comparing how the category travelled across languages. The architecture accepts new sources and a longer temporal window; a future iteration would use OpenAlex's bulk download rather than keyword queries, reducing dependence on vocabulary chosen at harvest time. By making its boundaries explicit rather than implicit, the corpus turns the definition of "climate finance" from a hidden assumption into an object of analysis.

## Data and Code Availability {.unnumbered}

The corpus data files and pipeline source code are deposited in Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 at [10.5281/zenodo.19236130](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19236130). Key software dependencies: Python $\geq$ 3.10, pandas, sentence-transformers, and DVC. Suggested citation:

> Ha-Duong, M. (2026). A Curated Corpus of Climate Finance Literature, 1990–2024: Six Sources, Multilingual Retrieval, and Grey Literature [Data set]. Zenodo. [10.5281/zenodo.19236130](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19236130)
